title: Freedom That Shows Up as Love
overview: Paul urges the believers in Galatia not to trade their freedom in Christ for rule-keeping, and to use that freedom to love and serve one another by the Spirit.

parts.label: Do not go back (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: Some teachers were telling non-Jewish believers they had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to be right with God, and Paul calls this a yoke, the heavy wooden beam put on working animals. He says making circumcision a requirement means leaning on rule-keeping instead of Christ, when what counts is faith that shows itself in love.

parts.label: Who tripped you up? (vv. 7-12)
parts.note: Paul pictures them as runners someone cut in front of, and compares the new teaching to a little yeast that spreads through the whole batch of dough. He notes he is still persecuted, which shows he does not preach circumcision, and his wish that the agitators would castrate themselves is openly crude, angry sarcasm.

parts.label: Free to serve (vv. 13-15)
parts.note: Freedom is not permission to feed "the flesh," Paul's term for self-centered human nature, but a chance to serve each other in love. He sums up the whole law as loving your neighbor as yourself, and his picture of biting and devouring suggests real quarrels were already happening.

parts.label: An inner tug of war (vv. 16-21)
parts.note: Paul describes a conflict between selfish desires and God's Spirit, the presence of God living in believers, and says those led by the Spirit are not under the law. His list includes sexual wrongs, false worship, magic and drunkenness, but much of it is about relationships breaking down, and he warns that people who live this way will not inherit God's kingdom.

parts.label: What the Spirit grows (vv. 22-26)
parts.note: Paul calls love, joy, peace and the rest the "fruit" of the Spirit and says no law stands against such things; many readers take the singular word to mean one crop the Spirit grows rather than a checklist of efforts. Having "crucified the flesh" means treating the old self-centered life as put to death with Christ, and Paul closes by warning against pride and envy.

disagreement: Christians differ on what Paul is mainly opposing: many read it as any attempt to earn God's acceptance through good deeds, while others read it more narrowly as requiring non-Jewish believers to adopt Jewish markers like circumcision in order to belong.
think: When has feeling free in your own life made you more generous toward other people, and when has it made you less so?
